Gulf exports accelerate prompting funds to sell oil

Investors sold petroleum for the second week running anticipating crude and fuel exports through the Strait of Hormuz and via pipelines will normalise even without a formal ceasefire between the United States and Iran.

Saudi Arabia has partially repaired and restarted the East-West Petroline damaged by drone attacks in September, permitting the resumption of crude exports via the Red Sea.

Crude exports have also accelerated via the Strait itself, with more tankers transiting the waterway under cover of darkness with their automatic identification systems switched off, under sea and air protection from the United States.

The system of shuttling crude oil through the Strait and reloading it in the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea for onward transport to refiners in Asia appears to have become increasingly effective ...

Refined products: Following political pressure from the US, the G7 said it plans to release 100 million barrels of crude and diesel over the next four months. While this provided some short-term relief on Friday, the release may not be enough to drive spreads to crude materially lower, with the Brent-gas oil spread currently around USD 77/bbl from a recent peak near USD 100/bbl and around USD 25/bbl this time last year. 

It does little to address the structural constraints facing the refined-products market, including shrinking Russian supply, curtailed Middle East exports and China's suspension of fuel exports for October. Together, these developments risk keeping distillate markets tight and prices elevated as the Northern Hemisphere enters the peak winter demand season. 

The ICE gasoil futures contract, the main feedstock for diesel, jet fuel and heating oil slumped 6.6% on Friday to near a one-month low, before trading higher this morning while Brent is lower.

COT on #commodities: Managed money remained firmly on the defensive in the week to 29 September as a stronger dollar and surging US Treasury yields helped drive the Bloomberg Commodity Index down 2.1%.
Funds sold 18 of 25 major commodity futures, led by crude oil, natural gas, gold, silver, soybeans and corn. The combined WTI and Brent net long fell 31k contracts to a five-week low.
Gold continues to highlight a notable divergence: hedge funds cut 2.7 million ounces of exposure during September, while ETF investors added 1.7 million ounces, lifting holdings to a four-year high.
Agriculture positioning remains relatively sticky, with a 6% price decline since early September triggering only an 11% reduction in the record net long.

#Agriculture: The @UNFAO Food Price Index averaged 136 points in September, reaching a 4½-year high and rising 5.8% year-on-year. The increase was driven primarily by strong gains in sugar (+6.1%) and cereals (+5.1%), with vegetable oils (+0.9%) also contributing. Meat prices (-1.1%) were the only major component to decline last month, while dairy prices were broadly unchanged.

Highlights from the report: 
The FAO Cereal Price Index rose sharply in September, driven by tightening supply and growing logistical risks. Wheat prices were supported by Black Sea export constraints, which pushed buyers towards alternative origins, as well as dry weather ahead of North American winter wheat planting. Maize also strengthened as disappointing US yields, reduced Brazilian export availability and Black Sea disruptions tightened the supply outlook. Elevated fuel, fertiliser and freight costs linked to uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz added further support, particularly for crops with biofuel exposure. Rice prices edged higher on weather concerns and seasonally tighter supplies.

The FAO Vegetable Oil Price Index rose modestly, led by palm oil, where strong import demand and concerns about dry weather affecting Southeast Asian production outweighed weakness elsewhere. Sunflower oil declined on expectations of ample Black Sea supplies, although logistical constraints limited the downside. Soy oil remained supported by robust biofuel demand.

The FAO Meat Price Index declined as ample supplies weighed on poultry and pork. Brazilian poultry exports faced softer EU demand following new import requirements, while increased pig meat availability across major producing regions pressured prices. Beef and sheep meat prices were broadly stable, with regional differences reflecting shifts in demand, trade policy and currency movements.

The FAO Dairy Price Index was broadly unchanged. Strong Asian demand and limited prompt availability supported milk powder prices, while cheese weakened amid softer European demand, strong US export competition and rising seasonal supply from Oceania. Butter was little changed, with tighter European milkfat availability offsetting weaker prices elsewhere.

The FAO Sugar Price Index rose strongly as the market priced a tighter global supply outlook. Smaller EU beet acreage and adverse weather, weaker production prospects in Thailand, concerns about India's crop amid below-normal rainfall and developing El Niño conditions, and harvest disruptions caused by heavy rain in Brazil all contributed to the increase.
